newsitem.title: IRAQ: Iraqis protest against U.N. sanctions.
newsitem.headline: Iraqis protest against U.N. sanctions.

text.p: Hundreds of Iraqi trade unionists on Tuesday organised rallies in front of a U.N. office in Baghdad to protest against U.N. trade sanctions on Iraq.
Workers, women and students chanted slogans lashing out at the United States, blaming it for the trade sanctions imposed on Iraq after its troops invaded Kuwait in 1990.
A senior Iraqi official on Tuesday criticised the U.N. Security Council for delaying permission for Iraq to use helicopters to fight agricultural pests and diseases.
Basel Kamel Dalali, undersecretary at the Agriculture Ministry, also called on the French government to do more to have all U.N. sanctions lifted.

"We are still waiting for permission to use aircraft to fight pests and (agricultural) diseases...This (ban on use of planes) is an unjust act and has no legal or technical justification," said Dalali while opening an agriculture and food products exhibition organised by French companies.
The sanctions also include a ban on airlines flying to Iraq. In the past, Iraq has been able to obtain permission from the U.N. committee to allow it to use helicopters for agricultural means.

Iraq is under two no-fly zones in its north and south. The one in the north is imposed by the United States and Britain while the southern no-fly zone is guarded by French, British and U.S. warplanes.
"We wish that the French government and friendly countries double their political and humanitarian efforts to lift these unjustifiable incursions (sanctions on Iraq)," Dalali said.

He lauded France's decision to withdraw from patrolling the no-fly-zone in north Iraq last month, saying that "Iraqi leadership is giving preference to French firms among the western companies (in concluding trade deals)".
Fifty French agriculture and food producers, among them Serac, Adepta, Bayle, Sodiaal, Emery, Soviba and others, are displaying their products at Baghdad's al-Rasheed Hotel.

The French firms are seeking to sell their products to Iraq under an oil-for-food deal signed with the United Nations. The deal, concluded on December 10, allows Baghdad to sell $2 billion worth of oil every six months to buy food and medicine for Iraqis.
France's was Iraq's main Western trade partner before Iraq invaded Kuwait in 1990. Baghdad owes Paris more than $5 billion and the French are keen to restore economic ties once the embargo is lifted.
France irked Iraq this month by refusing to give medical treatment on French territory to President Saddam Hussein's eldest son Uday, who was wounded by unidentified gunmen in Baghdad on December 12.
